**Understanding the problem**
Same setting as 3425, but now a downward path is special if all values are distinct **except at most one value may appear twice**. Return the maximum path length and, among maximum-length paths, the minimum node count.

**Example 1:** Paths 1→2→4 (values 1,0,1) and 1→3→6→8 (values 1,3,1,0) each contain exactly one duplicated value and have length 9; the latter has 4 nodes, the former 3, so the answer is `[9,3]`. **Example 2:** 0→3 has distinct values, length 5, 2 nodes → `[5,2]`.

Same DFS framework as 3425, but the allowed-start computation must tolerate one duplicate.
k: Keeping the last TWO occurrences of each value on the current path suffices: starting after the second-to-last occurrence leaves at most one copy of that value.
Taking the maximum allowed-start over all values guarantees at most one duplicated value survives on the path.
Everything else (prefix distances, monotone starts, answer update) is identical to problem 3425.

a.i: Maintain the root path and, per value, the stack of depths where it occurs. On entering v, if nums[v] occurred before at depths p1 < p2 (the two most recent), a path ending at v may start at depth p2+1: it then contains exactly the two latest copies of nums[v] and at most one copy of any other value (any other duplicated pair would have forced an even later start). With no prior occurrence, start at the root. Distances increase downward, so the earliest allowed start maximizes length.
s: Build adjacency; DFS from root carrying prefix distance and the path stack.
Per value keep the list of occurrence depths on the current path.
Allowed start = (second-to-last occurrence depth of nums[v]) + 1, or 0 if fewer than two occurrences.
Update the answer with length dist[v] − dist[startNode] and node count; pop state on backtrack.
a.t: O(n) — one DFS; each node pushes/pops once and each hash lookup is O(1) amortized.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency, path stack, distances, and occurrence lists (total occurrences across values ≤ n).

**Wrap-up**
This is a one-line delta from problem 3425: replace "last occurrence + 1" with "second-to-last occurrence + 1". Pitfalls: using the *latest* occurrence instead of the second-to-latest (that bans the very duplicate we're allowed); forgetting that three copies of a value make earlier windows invalid (handled automatically since the start moves past the second copy); initializing the answer to `[0,1]` for single-node paths. Follow-up: allow k duplicated values — keep the last k+1 occurrences per value and start after the (k)-th-to-last.
